title: Alexander Zverev ends Arthur Féry’s Wimbledon run to reach second Grand Slam final in a row
content:
THE ALL ENGLAND CLUB, London — Arthur Féry’s barely believable Wimbledon run ended at the semifinal stage with defeat to world No. 2 Alexander Zverev Friday on Centre Court.

Féry, the British wild card ranked No. 114, had been defying gravity all fortnight, but ultimately found Zverev, the French Open champion, too big a step up in quality throughout a 7-6(0), 6-2, 6-4 defeat.

Zverev, 29, has seemingly been liberated by finally becoming a Grand Slam winner at Roland Garros last month. He played with authority and confidence, and showed the kind of aggressiveness on the forehand side that he has often pledged to do, but has rarely been able to do in practice. Twenty winners on that wing underlined how much Zverev was feeling the shot, especially against an opponent who has shown himself extremely difficult to hit through.

In the final, Zverev will be an underdog against either defending champion Jannik Sinner, against whom he has lost nine times in a row, or seven-time champion Novak Djokovic, but after that breakthrough in Paris, he’ll surely be able to play with far less pressure than in his previous four Grand Slam finals.

Féry’s remarkable run may be over, but his tournament has exceeded all expectations expect perhaps his own, given how remarkably unflustered he has been over the past couple of weeks.

Wimbledon 2026 has transformed his career, propelling him from world No. 114 to world No. 36, and having never previously made the main draw of a Grand Slam by ranking, he is suddenly on the verge of being seeded at the biggest events.

Féry turns 24 Sunday, but he is rookie in professional terms, having spent three years at Stanford University between 2020 and 2023 before largely managing injuries more than playing tennis. He has played as many matches in this event as he had previously at Grand Slam level in his career.

Where he goes from here is uncertain. For every player who kicks on after this kind of breakout run, there’s one who fairly swiftly retreats back to the margins. The main obstacle for Féry maintaining this kind of level would appear to be the suitability of his game for hard and clay courts, which make up the bulk of the tennis calendar. His fluid service motion makes up for his diminutive (for a tennis player) 5-feet-9-inches height, and his skidding backhand slice has been devastating on grass, but it remains to be seen how it will transfer to other surfaces.

He has plenty of time to try and develop his game in this regard, given that he has so few ranking points to defend in the rest of the year. A few wins at ATP Tour level could hoist him up to being seeded at the majors and ATP Masters 1000 events, let alone being an automatic entry for them.

Part of that process will involve trying to learn from the lesson he was given by one of the best players in the world on Centre Court.

Féry looked typically unflappable in the opening exchanges. He forced Zverev to deuce on the German’s first service game and then held to love himself. And even when Zverev grabbed an early break, Féry didn’t roll over against a player who had only been broken four times all tournament coming into their match.

He broke straight back for 3-2, including a point that electrified Centre Court as he chased down a Zverev drop shot and outmaneuvered his opponent with an angled backhand flick.

Zverev was getting around 75 percent of his first serves in, which usually spells game over for his opponent. But Féry was getting a read on it, returning one hit at 137 mph and winning the point with Zverev serving at 3-3. And despite the chasm in experience, it was Zverev who looked the edgier of the two players — just as Flavio Cobolli had done in his quarterfinal against Féry.

Unlike the Italian No. 9 seed, Zverev started to loosen up though and feel the ball, particularly on his much-improved forehand side. Previously the weaker and far more conservative wing for Zverev, he’s made a concerted effort to hit the shot more aggressively — and has rarely done so with more authority than towards the end of the first set and in the second on Friday. Zverev finished the opener with six forehand winners, and hit another nine in the second.

Despite Zverev lacing those winners, Féry did enough to force a first-set tiebreak. But at that point, Zverev did what a Grand Slam champion is supposed to do and raised his level. He made all three of his first serves, and hit a couple more bruising forehands on his way to winning it 7-0.

Féry’s remarkable ability to recover from losing positions this fortnight had the vast majority of Centre Court holding out hope for another famous comeback, but Zverev is a master of managing opponents ranked lower than him.

The game he played to break to love for 2-1 in the second set was described by John McEnroe in commentary for the BBC as “one of the best I’ve ever seen from him.” A bullet forehand return winner for 0-40 was the highlight, and all of a sudden, this semifinal it looked like the tennis version of a boxing match between fighters from different weight classes that was on paper.

When Zverev broke again for 4-1, helped by a sensational flicked forehand pass off a drop volley, he sucked any of the remaining crowd energy out of Centre Court. The expectation had been that this was going to be a tricky atmosphere for Zverev to deal with, but he’d pretty much taken the crowd out of the equation by dominating to the extent that he was. A lob at the start of the next game almost felt cruel.

Féry took a lengthy break at the end of the second set, but Zverev pretty much carried on from where he left off when they resumed. He broke for 3-2 with an inside out forehand hit with such ferocity that you couldn’t help wondering how much more Zverev could have achieved in his career if he’d started to hit the shot with this kind of power and bravery a few years ago.

It looked to be all over when Zverev had three break points for 5-2, but Féry gave the Centre Court crowd something to cheer about at last. He saved them all, the last with a sublime half-volley passing shot that earned him applause even from Zverev. And then banged down a couple of aces for the hold. Centre Court was as loud as it had been all afternoon, willing Féry to pull off another miraculous comeback, like the ones against Zizou Bergs and Grigor Dimitrov in the third and fourth round.

Zverev slammed the door shut one last time though, holding serve a couple more times to reach a first Wimbledon final, meaning he’s reached the final of all four Slams.

Féry left the court to warm applause, surely believing that this was no aberration and will be the start of something big for him. And with Jack Draper and Emma Raducanu battling injuries, British tennis may have found itself a very unlikely hero.
